title: Asthma: Prove Variable Airflow Disease, Then Control Risk
bottomLine: Asthma is a variable airway disease diagnosed from a compatible symptom pattern plus objective evidence of variable airflow limitation when feasible. Management addresses current symptoms and future exacerbation risk, preserves inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, and escalates only after confirming diagnosis, adherence, technique and triggers.
recognize: Episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness and dyspnea that vary over time and triggers support asthma.
A normal exam or spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma.
differentiate: COPD has persistent airflow obstruction in the correct exposure context; vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure, PE and anxiety can mimic asthma symptoms.
A bronchodilator response supports variability but is not the only way to establish asthma.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, night waking, reliever use, exacerbations/systemic steroids, smoking/vaping, allergens/occupation, pregnancy and comorbid rhinitis/reflux/obesity.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator testing when possible; use peak-flow variability or bronchoprovocation when diagnosis remains uncertain and the clinical pathway supports it.
Do not leave chronic asthma on symptoms alone without objective confirmation when testing is feasible.
management: Use current CTS asthma guidance with an ICS-containing controller strategy and written action plan; step up or down based on control/risk after checking technique/adherence.
Severe or atypical disease, frequent exacerbations or biologic consideration warrants specialty referral.
medicationSafety: Frequent short-acting reliever or repeated oral steroid use signals poor control and treatment risk rather than a successful plan.
redFlags: Prior ICU/intubation with current severe symptoms
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, trigger reduction, action-plan zones and when an exacerbation requires urgent care.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbation risk, inhaler technique and adherence after treatment changes and after acute attacks.
examTrap: Escalating controller intensity before checking whether the diagnosis, inhaler technique and adherence are actually correct.
oneLinePearl: Asthma treatment starts with proving variability and fixing technique before adding complexity.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current asthma guideline and tools

title: COPD: Confirm Persistent Obstruction, Then Treat Symptoms and Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: COPD requires persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in the right exposure/clinical context. Management is driven by symptoms, exacerbation history and phenotype—not FEV1 alone—and combines smoking cessation, vaccination, inhaled therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation and exacerbation planning.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and recurrent exacerbations in a smoking/exposure history raise probability.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency should be considered according to current Canadian targeted-testing guidance.
differentiate: Asthma has variable airflow disease and can coexist with COPD; heart failure, ILD, obesity/deconditioning and bronchiectasis can mimic or worsen dyspnea.
A single pre-bronchodilator obstructive tracing is not enough to establish COPD.
assessment: Assess dyspnea/function, exacerbation/hospital history, eosinophil/asthma features where relevant, smoking, inhaler technique, oxygenation, weight/nutrition and comorbidity.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with quality post-bronchodilator spirometry and use imaging/labs for alternative or additional diagnoses when indicated.
management: Use current CTS stable-COPD pharmacotherapy guidance matched to symptom and exacerbation burden, plus smoking cessation, exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination.
Use an action plan for exacerbations and reassess after hospitalization or frequent steroid/antibiotic use.
medicationSafety: ICS-containing therapy is not automatically indicated for every COPD patient and increases pneumonia/thrush risk; asthma/eosinophilic/exacerbation context matters.
Long-acting bronchodilator combinations require inhaler/device review and adherence assessment before escalation.
counselling: Teach smoking cessation, inhaler technique, physical activity and individualized exacerbation warning signs.
followUp: Track symptoms/function, exacerbations, inhaler use and spirometry when it will change management.
examTrap: Calling COPD from symptoms without post-bronchodilator obstruction—or treating FEV1 as the only determinant of therapy.
oneLinePearl: COPD is confirmed by persistent obstruction and managed by symptoms plus exacerbation risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 stable COPD pharmacotherapy guideline

title: Pneumonia: Community vs Healthcare Exposure Changes the Empiric Plan
bottomLine: Pneumonia treatment begins by confirming a compatible lower-respiratory syndrome, assessing severity and identifying epidemiologic/healthcare exposures that change resistant-pathogen risk. Community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia should not be treated as interchangeable labels, and antibiotics should be narrowed or stopped when evidence changes.
recognize: Fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia and focal chest findings with compatible imaging support pneumonia.
Older/frail adults may present with delirium or functional decline rather than classic fever.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis usually lacks focal pneumonia physiology/imaging and generally does not benefit from antibiotics.
Aspiration pneumonitis, PE, heart failure and viral infection can mimic bacterial pneumonia.
assessment: Assess severity, oxygenation, hemodynamics, aspiration risk, immune status, recent hospitalization/antibiotics, prior resistant organisms and pregnancy.
workup: Use chest imaging when pneumonia is clinically suspected and severity/diagnostic uncertainty warrants it; obtain cultures for severe disease or when resistant-pathogen information will change care.
Do not obtain indiscriminate cultures in low-risk uncomplicated outpatient CAP.
management: Choose empiric therapy according to setting, severity, comorbidity, prior microbiology and local guidance; define duration/reassessment and narrow when clinical/microbiologic evidence permits.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia requires a healthcare-associated pathogen/risk assessment rather than routine outpatient CAP therapy.
medicationSafety: Check allergy, renal/hepatic function, QT/drug interactions and C. difficile risk when choosing antibiotics.
Avoid unnecessarily broad or prolonged therapy when the patient is improving and microbiology supports de-escalation.
counselling: Teach expected recovery and clear return precautions; persistent symptoms should trigger reassessment rather than automatic antibiotic extension.
followUp: Review clinical response and pending microbiology; ensure repeat imaging only when indicated by persistent symptoms/high-risk features.
examTrap: Using the same outpatient CAP regimen for a deteriorating hospital-acquired pneumonia without assessing resistant-pathogen risk.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia antibiotics follow syndrome, severity and exposure history—not one universal recipe.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory antibiotic stewardship

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Probability First, Then Hemodynamic Risk
bottomLine: PE care has two separate risk questions: first, how likely is PE and what diagnostic strategy is appropriate; second, once PE is diagnosed, is the patient hemodynamically high risk, intermediate risk or low risk for disposition/treatment planning. D-dimer is a rule-out tool in selected patients, not a severity marker.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope and DVT findings can occur; no single symptom is diagnostic.
Hypotension/shock, severe RV strain or clinical deterioration defines a different treatment pathway from stable low-risk PE.
differentiate: Low/intermediate pretest probability may permit D-dimer-based exclusion; high clinical probability generally proceeds to imaging rather than using a negative strategy indiscriminately.
Pregnancy/postpartum PE uses pregnancy-appropriate diagnostic and anticoagulation pathways.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, bleeding risk, pregnancy, renal function, cancer, prior VTE, provoking factors and medications.
workup: Use validated clinical probability plus D-dimer/imaging strategies; once diagnosed, assess clinical risk and RV injury/strain when it changes disposition or reperfusion decisions.
management: Start anticoagulation promptly when indicated and safe; stable low-risk PE may qualify for outpatient treatment after structured risk/social assessment.
High-risk PE is an emergency requiring immediate acute-care/reperfusion evaluation; intermediate-risk disease requires close monitored assessment rather than routine outpatient discharge.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant selection depends on pregnancy, renal function, bleeding risk, cancer, interactions and adherence/access.
Do not use thrombolysis simply because clot burden looks large on CT without the hemodynamic/risk context.
counselling: Teach bleeding precautions, recurrence symptoms, adherence and when emergency reassessment is required.
followUp: Define anticoagulation duration using provoking/recurrent-risk and bleeding-risk assessment and close the loop on cancer/persistent dyspnea evaluation when indicated.
examTrap: Using D-dimer as a severity marker after PE is diagnosed—or giving thrombolysis for a stable patient because the CT looks dramatic.
oneLinePearl: PE probability guides diagnosis; hemodynamic risk guides treatment intensity.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada PE diagnosis, treatment and high/intermediate-risk clinical guides

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Sinusitis: Treat the Syndrome, Not Every Coloured Secretion
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory upper-airway syndrome treated with trigger control and effective intranasal therapy, while most acute rhinosinusitis is viral/self-limited. Antibiotics require a defensible bacterial pattern or complication risk—not mucus colour alone.
recognize: Sneezing, itching, watery rhinorrhea and congestion with seasonal/perennial triggers support allergic rhinitis.
Bacterial sinusitis becomes more plausible with persistent/worsening severe patterns rather than the first few days of a cold.
differentiate: Viral URI, nonallergic rhinitis, medication rebound, dental disease and migraine can mimic sinus symptoms.
Orbital/intracranial complications are emergencies, not outpatient 'sinus infection' management.
assessment: Assess duration/pattern, fever, facial pain, dental symptoms, allergy triggers, asthma, medication/decongestant use and orbital/neurologic symptoms.
workup: Routine imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis or allergic rhinitis; image/refer when complications, mass, recurrent atypical disease or chronic-refractory symptoms warrant it.
management: Use intranasal corticosteroid and/or antihistamine strategies for allergic rhinitis with technique teaching and allergen measures.
Use supportive care for likely viral sinusitis and reserve antibiotics for guideline-consistent bacterial disease.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestant overuse can cause rebound rhinitis; oral decongestants can worsen hypertension/arrhythmia and have pregnancy considerations.
Avoid repeated antibiotic courses without confirming the syndrome.
counselling: Explain that green/yellow discharge can occur with viral infection and does not by itself mean antibiotics are needed.
followUp: Reassess persistent/recurrent symptoms for chronic rhinosinusitis, structural disease or uncontrolled allergy/asthma.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because nasal discharge changed colour on day four of an uncomplicated URI.
oneLinePearl: Sinus antibiotics need a bacterial pattern, not just coloured mucus.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory/primary-care antibiotic stewardship

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Look for Lung Disease Before Antibiotics
bottomLine: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and self-limited; antibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated disease. The NP task is to identify pneumonia, pertussis, asthma/COPD exacerbation or another important alternative using vitals, lung examination, host risk and targeted imaging when indicated.
recognize: Cough may last weeks after acute bronchitis and sputum colour does not reliably distinguish bacterial infection.
Pneumonia becomes more likely with abnormal vitals, hypoxemia, focal lung findings, frailty or systemic illness.
differentiate: Wheeze may represent viral bronchitis or unrecognized asthma/COPD; pertussis has a prolonged paroxysmal/post-tussive pattern.
PE and heart failure can mimic lower-respiratory symptoms and should be considered when the story does not fit infection.
assessment: Assess duration, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, oxygenation, respiratory/heart rate, focal findings, comorbidity, pregnancy and pertussis/exposure risk.
workup: Use chest radiography when pneumonia cannot be reasonably excluded from the clinical assessment or the host is high risk; avoid routine imaging in a stable low-risk bronchitis syndrome.
management: Provide symptom care and return precautions for uncomplicated bronchitis; do not routinely prescribe antibiotics.
Treat confirmed/suspected pneumonia or pertussis according to the appropriate pathway and severity.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and opioid antitussives; both can cause harm without treating uncomplicated viral bronchitis.
Bronchodilators are not routine for every cough but may help when bronchospasm/airflow disease is present.
counselling: Set expectations that cough can persist after viral illness and explain the specific symptoms that should trigger reassessment.
followUp: Reassess worsening or nonresolving cough for pneumonia, pertussis, asthma/COPD, malignancy or another alternate diagnosis.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for coloured sputum in a stable patient with normal vitals and no focal pneumonia findings.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is usually a cough problem; pneumonia is a lung-injury problem that needs evidence.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory antibiotic stewardship
